Assert that observations lie within each unit's lifetime

Source: R/ensure_within.R
ensure_within.Rd

A checkpoint for rows that cannot exist: a person observed after death, after emigrating, or before being born; a company with income after it was dissolved. They come from linking registers updated at different times, and from late corrections: a death registered after the extract was made. Each row's time must lie within its own from and to, columns of the data such as the birth date and the date of death. On failure the offending rows are reported with an outside column prepended that says which bound they break. Returns data, so it can sit in the middle of a pipeline.

Usage

ensure_within(
  data,
  time,
  from = NULL,
  to = NULL,
  success_msg = NULL,
  warn_msg = NULL,
  abort_msg = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A data frame or tibble, a database table (dbplyr, e.g. DuckDB) or an Arrow table or dataset; see Database and Arrow tables.

time

Column with the period or date of each row (tidy-select), e.g. year.

from, to

Columns with the first and last period or date the unit can be observed, e.g. birth_date and death_date. At least one is required.

success_msg

Message shown when the rule holds. If NULL (default), it is "Check passed: <message>" when warn_msg or abort_msg is given, so the console names every check that ran, and a description of the check otherwise.

warn_msg

Message shown when rows lie outside and no abort_msg is set. Defaults to a description of the check.

abort_msg

If provided, cli::cli_abort() is called with this message when the rule is broken. If NULL (default), a warning is issued instead.

Value

data invisibly, unchanged.

Details

A missing bound is open: a person without a date of death is alive, and rows with a missing time are not checked. Bounds are inclusive, so an observation on the day of death is within.

Years against dates

time and the bounds may be dates or whole numbers such as years, in any combination. When one side is a year and the other a date, the date counts by its year: a yearly panel row for 2024 is within for a person who died in March 2024, and outside for one who died in 2023. Two dates are compared by day, and two numbers as they are.

Bounds from another register

The bounds usually come from the population register, not from the data being checked. Join them on first:

income |>
  dplyr::left_join(population, by = "cpr") |>
  ensure_within(year, from = birth_date, to = death_date)

to is the final exit: death, or an emigration without return. A person who emigrates and comes back has a residence history, not one exit date; check rows against residence spells with add_spell_status() instead.

Why it is fast

Each bound is one compiled pass over the rows that returns only the rows outside it, with no vector as long as the data in between. A year meets a date through a table of the few years present, so the dates are never converted to years.

See also

checkpoints, describe_panel() for entries and exits per period.

Examples

panel <- data.frame(
  cpr   = c("a", "a", "a", "b", "b"),
  year  = c(2022, 2023, 2024, 2022, 2023),
  born  = as.Date(c("1950-04-01", "1950-04-01", "1950-04-01",
                    "2023-01-10", "2023-01-10")),
  death = as.Date(c("2023-05-01", "2023-05-01", "2023-05-01", NA, NA))
)
# a has a row after the year of death, b one before birth
ensure_within(panel, year, from = born, to = death)
#> Warning: Rows outside: year within born to death
#> ℹ 2 rows in 2 groups
#>   Bounds broken: after death (1), before born (1)
#> ℹ The rows:
#>     outside      year born       death      cpr
#>     <chr>       <dbl> <date>     <date>     <chr>
#>   1 after death  2024 1950-04-01 2023-05-01 a
#>   2 before born  2022 2023-01-10 NA         b
